newsitem.title: USA: ShopKo, Phar-Mor cancel $1 billion merger.
newsitem.headline: ShopKo, Phar-Mor cancel $1 billion merger.

text.p: Retailer ShopKo Stores Inc. and drugstore chain Phar-Mor Inc. Wednesday called off their planned $1 billion merger after failing to resolve key issues in the transaction.
The move marked the end of a deal announced seven months ago that had been fraught with problems and scepticism from the start.
The companies said in a joint statement that they cancelled the proposed deal because of "continuing uncertainties" that they did not specify.

"While we continue to believe that a strategic combination would make sense, it became clear that the transaction as contemplated was not likely to be completed and that the continuing uncertainty is not in the best interests of our shareholders," ShopKo Chief Executive Officer Dale P. Kramer said in a news release. ShopKo is based in Green Bay, Wis.

The companies, which have combined annual sales of $3.2 billion, planned to merge by creating a holding company that was to be called Cabot Noble Inc., with each of the two companies continuing to operate separately as subsidiaries.

But the transaction ran into trouble due to a decline in Phar-Mor's stock price, regulatory delays and uncertainty about the position of one large shareholder, industry experts and sources familiar with the companies said.
"There were many problems. Not all the pieces fell into place," said Jay Meltzer of LJR Redbook Research.

Wall Street had disliked it from the beginning, contending the companies were dissimilar and could not achieve sizable cost savings by merging. Phar-Mor, of Youngstown, Ohio, is a drugstore chain and ShopKo is a discount retailer with a healthcare subsidiary.
"I never understood it to start with. You had two businesses that had nothing to do with each other," said one investment banker who specialises in the retail sector.
Sources said the planned exchange of shares became a troubling issue when Phar-Mor's stock, which had been trading around $8 per share when the deal was set, declined to about $5.
The companies also had not received required approval from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
"It just became clear this thing was going to continue to drag on," said one source familiar with the situation.

Another sticking point was the uncertain position of key shareholder FoxMeyer Health Corp., sources said. Hamilton Morgan LLC, jointly owned by Phar-Mor Chairman Robert Haft and Foxmeyer, holds 40 percent of Phar-Mor shares.
At the time the deal was announced, the companies said Foxmeyer had not reached a conclusion as to its position on the transaction.
FoxMeyer could not be reached for comment.

Shares of both companies gained in Wednesday trading as the cloud of uncertainty about the deal was lifted. ShopKo stock jumped $1.25, or more than 8 percent, to $16.50, making it one of the biggest percentage gainers on the New York Stock Exchange in consolidated afternoon trading. Phar-Mor rose 37.5 cents to $5.375 on Nasdaq.
Both companies are expected to move quickly to find new opportunities.
"We will continue to pursue other strategic opportunities that will allow us to build on our market position and enhance the Phar-Mor concept," Haft said in the statement.
Meanwhile, shareholders of ShopKo are expected to learn more about the company's plans Thursday when it holds a telephone conference call after releasing earnings for its fiscal fourth quarter.

ShopKo wants to move quickly in order to enable Supervalu Inc., which owns 46 percent of ShopKo, to exit its investment. Under the merger plan, the new holding company would have bought out the bulk of Supervalu's holdings in ShopKo.

Supervalu bought ShopKo in 1971 and then sold 54 percent of its stock in a 1991 public offering. Supervalu said Wednesday it was committed to ending its investment in ShopKo, but supported the decision to terminate the Phar-Mor deal.
ShopKo operates 130 stores in 15 states stretching from the upper Midwest to the Pacific Northwest. Its ProVantage Inc. unit specialises in prescription, vision and health benefit services.
Phar-Mor operates 103 retail drug stores in 18 states, concentrated around Ohio, Pennsylvania and Virginia.
Supervalu's stock dropped 37.5 cents to $29.375 in consolidated NYSE trading.
